rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing truncation risk. This establishes the elution window and a baseline for testing gradient slope and temperature.

Double the gradient duration at the same temperature and solvent endpoints to identify slope-responsive critical pairs. The initial elution times suggest this should remain near the 10-minute scoring window.

Keep the successful shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity for the remaining near-coeluting pair. Higher temperature should also provide additional margin below the 10-minute time penalty.

Back off temperature by one step to move the newly critical late pair away from its apparent high-temperature convergence. This retains the shallower gradient and should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

At 60 C, slightly flatten the gradient to improve the remaining late critical pair while checking that the earlier marginal pair stays resolved. A two-minute increase should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

The longer gradient worsened the late critical pair, so shorten to 18 minutes to move it away from coelution. Monitor the earlier pair at R=1.61 in injection 3, which may become limiting as the gradient steepens.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to adjust selectivity and slightly flatten the gradient around the nearly fully resolved method. This tests whether the early marginal pair can reach baseline resolution without sacrificing the late pair or the sub-10-minute elution time.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 7 to improve both marginal early pairs. The late critical pair has some resolution margin, making this a promising balance for reaching full resolution below 10 minutes.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between injections 7 and 8, to balance the marginal early and late pairs. The lower endpoint remains above the observed elution window, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark while testing a shorter fully resolved separation. Raise the starting organic fraction and slightly flatten the gradient to offset the expected loss of early-pair resolution.

Retain injection 9 as the maximum-score method and test a different temperature-selectivity regime at its solvent settings. This may reveal a resolution margin that permits a faster fully resolved gradient.

Test a lower-temperature selectivity regime, since 50–55 C introduced close pairs while 40 C left only one unresolved pair in the scouting gradient. The slightly steeper gradient should limit retention time; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Lower temperature one step while holding the gradient fixed to test whether the two marginal early pairs separate in this selectivity regime. The previous last peak at 8.36 minutes leaves some margin before the time penalty; injection 9 remains the maximum-score method.

Return to the maximum-score conditions with a slightly steeper slope, 0.04583 versus 0.045 organic fraction per minute. This tests a small reduction in last-peak time while checking whether the early critical pairs retain R ≥ 1.5.

Test a narrower solvent window in the promising 30 C regime to spread the marginal early cluster while reducing initial retention. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this explores an alternative route to a faster fully resolved separation.

Slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 10 to improve its limiting early pair while retaining the faster, higher-organic start. Monitor the late pair’s resolution margin; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

At the solvent settings of injection 15, lower temperature to separate its limiting early pair, as the 25–30 C comparison suggests. Check whether the neighboring pair retains sufficient resolution; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the gradient at 25 C to shorten retention while testing whether the shallower slope resolves the remaining marginal pair from injection 17. Keep injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

Test whether warming the nearly resolved method from injection 18 separates its marginal pair while shortening retention. The early pair has enough resolution margin to justify testing this selectivity shift; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the nearly resolved 25 C method and reduce gradient slope to improve its remaining marginal pair. The last peak should remain near the 10-minute limit, potentially establishing another fully resolved method while preserving injection 9 as the benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fully resolved separation from injection 20. Its minimum resolution of 2.07 provides margin for this window adjustment; injection 9 remains the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Warm the fully resolved method from injection 21 by one step to shorten retention. Earlier temperature comparisons suggest this may improve its marginal central pair, while the neighboring pair has substantial resolution margin.

Return to 25 C and raise the starting organic fraction one step from fully resolved injection 21 to test a shorter separation. Monitor its marginal central pair closely; injection 9 remains the fastest established maximum-score method.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction moves the central pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation while shortening retention. Injection 9 remains the fastest established method with the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Raise the starting organic fraction one final step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation, checking for compression of the early peaks. Retain injection 24 as the fastest proven maximum-score method, with all pairs resolved and the last peak at 6.79 minutes.
